scorecard.title: William Lane Craig vs Peter Millican: Does God Exist?
scorecard.label: God and skeptical empiricism
scorecard.motion: Does the evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism?
scorecard.summary: Craig presented a cumulative Christian-theist case, while Millican challenged its warrants, specificity, and fit with contrary evidence; Millican's more consistently complete replies produced the higher locked score.
scorecard.sourceNote: This reconstruction uses the complete hash-locked transcript and events represented in the closed source packet, with the two representative quotations verified against audio.
scorecard.scoringNote: Scores are locked calculator outputs under the reassessment rubric: move dimensions were aggregated by importance within five preweighted sections, with no burden-completion adjustment for either side.

pro.text: the three facts that I mentioned are agreed upon by the majority of historians today
pro.context: Craig used this claim while replying to Millican's criticism of the resurrection sources, arguing that the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief retained substantial historical acceptance despite disputes about the gospel accounts.

con.text: the world we see just doesn't match up to what you'd expect from a perfect God
con.context: Millican stated this during his empirical argument from evil, contrasting observed suffering and purported divine morality with expectations generated by an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect Christian deity.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator

pro.words: Because the universe began to exist, it has a transcendent cause whose relation to time, space, and the causal regress requires it to be uncaused, timeless, changeless, spaceless, and immaterial.
pro.critique: strongest feature: Craig supplies an intelligible causal sequence from a finite cosmic beginning to a transcendent cause and identifies several attributes through explicit relations to time, space, matter, and regress. principal limitation: The evidence for a beginning and the warrant extending ordinary causal judgment to the universe remain compressed, while the listed attributes do not by themselves establish a personal Christian creator. live burden: He still must defend the causal principle in this unusual domain and bridge from an immaterial first cause to agency, moral perfection, and the specifically Christian hypothesis. locked score: The move earns 75, a strong but qualified result because its coherent subsidiary route materially advances the case while leaving important cosmological and theological bridges unresolved.

con.words: Ordinary causal experience concerns rearrangements of existing material and therefore does not justify extending the premise that whatever begins to exist has a cause to creation from nothing.
con.critique: strongest feature: Millican accurately isolates the causal premise, grants the argument's conditional validity, and explains why experience of material rearrangement may not warrant extrapolation to creation from nothing. principal limitation: The reply addresses only one indispensable component of Craig's cosmological case and does not independently undermine the claimed cosmic beginning or every route to a transcendent explanation. live burden: He must show that the difference between ordinary generation and cosmic origination defeats, rather than merely limits, the proposed causal principle while answering the remaining scientific and metaphysical supports. locked score: The move earns 78, a strong partial answer whose precise, charitable evidential challenge lands against a central premise but leaves two components and the broader cosmological inference standing.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity

pro.words: Life-permitting fine-tuning is extraordinarily improbable under chance, is not physically necessary, exhibits an independent pattern, and therefore is best explained by design.
pro.critique: strongest feature: Craig presents a recognizable comparative inference, distinguishes necessity, chance, and design, and connects narrow life-permitting ranges to a clearly stated subsidiary bridge supporting theism. principal limitation: His categorical rejection of necessity and chance outruns the supplied probability information, and his treatment of rival explanations understates uncertainty about parameter spaces, selection effects, and deeper physics. live burden: He must justify the relevant probability distribution, compare design with multiverse or physical-law hypotheses, and explain why the inferred designer favors the morally perfect Christian God. locked score: The move earns 71, a mixed but useful constructive because the route is clear and directly relevant while its evidential warrant, calibration, and representation of alternatives remain materially underdeveloped.

con.words: Fine-tuning warrants caution because humans readily over-detect purpose, cosmic probability judgments rest on one observed universe, deeper physics may explain the constants, and a multiverse would make life-permitting observation unsurprising.
con.critique: strongest feature: Millican contacts all four indispensable components of the fine-tuning case by challenging purpose detection, probability estimates, assumed physical contingency, and the neglect of multiverse selection effects. principal limitation: Several alternatives are presented as live possibilities rather than comparatively supported explanations, so their collective availability weakens Craig's inference more clearly than it establishes a superior naturalistic account. live burden: He must assign disciplined comparative weight to deeper physics and multiverse proposals, clarify their evidential independence, and show that caution changes the motion-level balance rather than only withholding certainty. locked score: The move earns 82, a strong full answer because its comprehensive, well-calibrated engagement substantially pressures the design inference despite a remaining evidential gap between possibility and probability.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil

pro.words: Objective moral values are evident in moral experience and, because they require God as their ground, their existence entails God's existence.
pro.critique: strongest feature: Craig states a compact moral syllogism and appeals to ordinary moral experience to make objective value a concrete evidential datum rather than an unexplained abstraction. principal limitation: The crucial grounding premise is asserted more than defended, the move does not exclude secular moral realism, and its generic conclusion lacks exact contact with the packet's locked Christian-theist route. live burden: He must explain why objective values or obligations require a divine person, answer non-theistic grounding accounts, and connect that ground to the character and identity specified by the motion. locked score: The move earns 62, a weak but recoverable contribution because its inference is understandable and topical while the decisive warrant, route contact, and comparative support remain insufficiently discharged.

con.words: The observed world's evil and purported divine morality do not match expectations for a perfect God, so the evidence favors skepticism and provides strong evidence against God's existence with very little in favor.
con.critique: strongest feature: Millican converts evil into comparative evidence by asking whether the observed world matches expectations under a morally perfect God, directly pressuring Craig's claim that morality supports theism. principal limitation: The move supplies limited detail about the distribution and severity of evil and does not fully compare its likelihood under theism with skeptical atheism after possible divine-purpose replies. live burden: He must defend the relevant expectations of perfect goodness, address freedom and soul-making explanations, and show that residual suffering materially shifts the complete cumulative comparison. locked score: The move earns 74, a mixed but substantial partial answer because its empirical counterpressure is coherent, clear, and route-relevant, although its evidential development and likelihood comparison remain compressed.

pro.words: The three facts used in Craig's resurrection inference are accepted by a majority of historians, and even Millican's cited skeptical scholars accept the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief.
pro.critique: strongest feature: Craig answers the source dispute with a concrete consensus claim and turns Millican's cited skeptical historians into support for the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of resurrection belief. principal limitation: The breadth, independence, and qualifications of that alleged agreement remain incompletely documented, and acceptance of three facts does not alone establish a supernatural explanation as best. live burden: He must substantiate the historical consensus, answer source dependence and discrepancies, and compare resurrection with natural explanations using criteria that do not assume the disputed divine cause. locked score: The move earns 73, a mixed but useful partial reply because it supports the factual basis of the inference while contacting only one component and leaving the explanatory leap unresolved.

con.words: The resurrection reports are late, non-eyewitness Christian advocacy documents; Matthew and Luke depend on Mark and another common source, and the accounts contain chronological and theological discrepancies, so they provide weak evidence for God.
con.critique: strongest feature: Millican identifies specific historiographic concerns—late advocacy sources, uncertain eyewitness status, literary dependence, and discrepancies—that materially reduce the claimed independence and reliability of the gospel record. principal limitation: The criticism narrows Craig's case to gospel reporting and contacts only one of four indispensable components, leaving other asserted evidence for appearances and early resurrection belief substantially unaddressed. live burden: He must engage the broader historical sources, distinguish damaging contradictions from ordinary variation, and show how the surviving record compares with natural and supernatural explanations. locked score: The move earns 75, a strong but bounded partial answer because its source criticism is precise and evidentially serious while its coverage and representation of the complete resurrection case remain incomplete.

sections.title: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden

pro.words: Religious disagreement does not discredit one common belief-forming method because religions do not share a single method, while Craig's own case uses logic, evidence, and personal experience.
pro.critique: strongest feature: Craig directly challenges the common-method premise behind Millican's disagreement argument and states why diverse religious practices need not discredit his combined use of experience, logic, and public evidence. principal limitation: He weakens Millican's claim about relevantly similar methods into a claim of complete methodological identity and offers little warrant that his own package is importantly more reliable. live burden: He must compare the reliability of shared experiential and testimonial mechanisms, explain how public arguments adjudicate incompatible revelations, and reconnect this reply to the cumulative motion-level case. locked score: The move earns 65, a mixed diagnostic reply because it contacts both target components but its evidential support, charity, and exact burden contact remain materially limited.

con.words: Even generously allowing disembodied mentality some prior probability, the specific omniperfect Christian God must compete with thousands of conflicting religious hypotheses, so absent an overwhelmingly strong case the rational conclusion is disbelief or at least agnosticism.
con.critique: strongest feature: Millican squarely addresses the motion by distinguishing generic disembodied mentality from the specific omniperfect Christian God and placing that hypothesis among numerous religious competitors requiring comparative support. principal limitation: The allocation of prior probability is largely asserted, and the move slides between agnosticism and disbelief without fully explaining when underdetermination warrants either conclusion. live burden: He must justify the comparison class, specify reasonable evidential thresholds, and demonstrate that Craig's cumulative evidence fails relative to both skeptical atheism and the strongest rival religious hypotheses. locked score: The move earns 75, a strong motion-level constructive because it frames the specificity burden fairly and clearly, while its probability model and final doxastic transition remain materially underwarranted.

strengths: Craig offered a clearly organized cumulative case spanning cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, resurrection evidence, and religious experience.
His cosmological opening articulated a recoverable causal route and carefully specified several proposed attributes of a transcendent cause.
His fine-tuning constructive clearly separated necessity, chance, and design as rival explanatory categories.
His resurrection reply supplied a concrete historian-consensus claim and directly used skeptical scholars cited by Millican.

blunders.text: Craig repeatedly moved from intelligible subsidiary inferences to stronger conclusions—especially a personal Christian creator—without fully defending the necessary probability, grounding, or specificity bridges.

strengths: Millican isolated the domain shift between ordinary material causation and creation from nothing without misrepresenting Craig's conditional argument.
His fine-tuning reply contacted every indispensable component through probability uncertainty, deeper physics, purpose detection, and multiverse selection.
His resurrection criticism identified concrete questions about source date, eyewitness status, literary dependence, and discrepancies.
His motion-level framing distinguished generic disembodied mentality from the specific omniperfect Christian hypothesis and demanded comparative support.

blunders.text: Millican sometimes relied on the availability of deeper physics, multiverse scenarios, or rival hypotheses without supplying enough comparative evidence to establish their probability or a uniquely atheistic conclusion.

newArguments.title: Specified likelihood ledger
newArguments.text: Construct a public likelihood ledger listing, for every evidential line, the Christian-theist prediction, the strongest naturalistic prediction, the disputed background assumptions, and a conservative likelihood range. Then combine only evidential contributions that remain after dependence is discounted. This would turn the cumulative appeal into an auditable comparison and reveal whether cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, resurrection evidence, and experience genuinely converge rather than merely repeat a shared prior commitment.

novelty.explanation: The proposal repairs the cumulative case by supplying transparent comparison and dependence controls.

newArguments.title: Layered specificity bridge
newArguments.text: Separate the conclusion into successive layers: a cause of the universe, purposive agency, morally significant agency, and the God identified by Christian revelation. Assign each layer its own evidence and rival hypotheses, allowing later historical or experiential evidence to update only the layers it actually bears upon. This prevents cosmological or fine-tuning evidence from carrying more theological specificity than it supports while preserving a route by which several different kinds of evidence can jointly narrow the hypothesis.

novelty.explanation: This directly repairs the recurring gap between generic-cause evidence and Christian specificity.

thesis.text: Skeptical atheism is strengthened when the Christian hypothesis is evaluated through explicit comparative predictions, alternative explanations, and penalties for theological flexibility.

novelty.explanation: This extends Millican's specificity and expectation arguments into one comparative method.

premises.text: A specific omniperfect Christian God generates stronger expectations than generic supernatural agency and therefore bears a correspondingly more demanding evidential test.

novelty.explanation: This develops the cited move's distinction between generic mentality and Christian theism.

premises.text: Natural alternatives weaken a theistic inference only when their mechanisms, prior plausibility, and predictive fit are compared rather than merely named.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the transcript's reliance on several possible but incompletely supported alternatives.

premises.text: Evil and divine hiddenness matter evidentially when their observed patterns are less expected under perfect goodness than under indifferent natural processes.

novelty.explanation: This formalizes the expectation comparison already present in Millican's empirical argument.

premises.text: Religious disagreement reduces testimonial and experiential weight when incompatible traditions arise through relevantly similar belief-forming mechanisms.

novelty.explanation: This preserves and clarifies the similar-method claim challenged during the exchange.

conclusion.text: If Christian theism predicts the total evidence no better than specified alternatives, while evil, hiddenness, and religious disagreement remain comparatively unexpected, withholding belief or adopting skeptical atheism is proportionate.

novelty.explanation: This clarifies the evidential conditions separating agnosticism from a stronger skeptical conclusion.

newArguments.title: Flexibility penalty
newArguments.text: Evaluate whether theological explanations predict observations in advance or accommodate nearly any outcome after the fact. If prosperity and suffering, clarity and hiddenness, or answered and unanswered prayer can all be reconciled with perfect divine purposes without independent constraints, the hypothesis gains limited predictive credit. Applying a flexibility penalty would sharpen Millican's argument from evil by distinguishing genuine expectation from retrospective compatibility and would specify what evidence could count against the Christian hypothesis.

novelty.explanation: The transcript did not explicitly formulate a penalty for unconstrained explanatory flexibility.

newArguments.title: Alternative-hypothesis matrix
newArguments.text: Build a matrix comparing Christian theism, impersonal deism, morally neutral design, multiverse cosmology, deeper physical law, and ordinary naturalism across every evidential category. Record where each hypothesis predicts the datum, merely permits it, or requires auxiliary assumptions. This would improve Millican's appeal to many competitors by replacing their raw number with a structured comparison, while also showing whether any single alternative must explain everything or whether different observations legitimately support different components of a skeptical model.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the rival-hypothesis argument by adding explicit comparative predictions and assumptions.
